q-sva-each.label: Each, every, either, neither
q-sva-each.summary: Each, every, either, neither and words like everyone take a singular verb.

q-sva-nearer.label: Either...or, neither...nor
q-sva-nearer.summary: With either...or and neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

q-sva-number.label: The number of / a number of
q-sva-number.summary: 'The number of' is singular; 'a number of' is plural.

q-sva-phrase.label: Along with, as well as
q-sva-phrase.summary: The verb agrees with the first subject, not with the noun after 'along with' or 'as well as'.

q-sva-spot.label: Subject far from its verb
q-sva-spot.summary: Long sentences put phrases between the subject and the verb, or make a whole clause the subject; find the real subject and check the verb.

q-sva-inverted.label: Verb before its subject
q-sva-inverted.summary: After 'so + adjective', 'here', 'there' and similar openers the verb comes first; it still agrees with the subject that follows.

q-sva-oneidea.label: Two nouns joined by 'and' naming one thing
q-sva-oneidea.summary: Two nouns or adjectives joined by 'and' take a singular verb when together they name one person, thing or idea, not two separate ones.

q-sva-fixedplural.label: Diseases, games, countries, subjects ending in -s
q-sva-fixedplural.summary: Some nouns that end in -s name one disease, game, country or field of study and take a singular verb: measles, billiards, the United States, Mathematics, Economics, Statistics.

q-sva-ofthe.label: 'One of the' + plural noun + singular verb
q-sva-ofthe.summary: 'One of the' is always followed by a plural noun, even though the verb that goes with 'one' itself stays singular.

q-sva-unit.label: A number + a plural noun of amount as a single unit
q-sva-unit.summary: A number of money, distance, weight, time or height, treated as a single amount rather than separate items, takes a singular verb.

q-sva-both.label: Both ... and always takes a plural verb
q-sva-both.summary: Two subjects joined by 'both ... and' always take a plural verb, with no exception for a nearer singular subject.

rules.text: Each, every, either, neither, everyone, everybody, nobody and anyone take a singular verb, even when 'of' plus a plural noun follows.
rules.ok: Each of the boys was rewarded.
rules.bad: Each of the boys were rewarded.

rules.text: When subjects are joined by either...or, neither...nor, or, nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it.
rules.ok: Neither the teacher nor the students were aware.
rules.bad: Neither the teacher nor the students was aware.

rules.text: 'The number of' + plural noun takes a singular verb (it is about the number). 'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb (it means 'many').
rules.ok: The number of cases is rising. A number of cases are pending.
rules.bad: The number of cases are rising.

rules.text: With, along with, together with, as well as, in addition to and besides do not add to the subject. The verb agrees with the first subject.
rules.ok: The principal, along with the teachers, is attending.
rules.bad: The principal, along with the teachers, are attending.

rules.text: A clause used as the subject ('That ...', 'What ...', 'Whether ...') takes a singular verb, however many plural nouns sit inside it.
rules.ok: That the reports were late was surprising.
rules.bad: That the reports were late were surprising.

rules.text: The verb agrees with the subject, never with the complement. 'Much of ...' and other uncountable subjects are singular even if a plural noun follows the verb.
rules.ok: Much of what he said is rumour.
rules.bad: Much of what he said are rumours.

rules.text: Cross out the phrases between commas and the prepositional phrases after the subject, then match the verb to the noun left. 'The focus on X' is singular, however plural X is.
rules.ok: The focus on small farms, though praiseworthy, ignores big ones.
rules.bad: The focus on small farms, though praiseworthy, ignore big ones.

rules.text: When the sentence opens with 'so + adjective' (or here, there, never ...), the verb comes before its subject and still agrees with the subject that follows it; also keep the tense the rest of the sentence needs.
rules.ok: So fragile were the talks that one leak could end them.
rules.bad: So fragile was the talks that one leak could end them.

rules.text: Two nouns or adjectives joined by 'and' take a singular verb when together they name one person, thing or idea rather than two. One test: if an article (a/the) stands only before the first of the pair, the pair is one thing, so the verb is singular; if the article is repeated before each one, they are different things, so the verb is plural.
rules.ok: Slow and steady wins the race.
rules.bad: Slow and steady win the race.

rules.text: Some nouns that end in -s and look plural in fact name one disease (measles, mumps, rickets, shingles), one game (billiards, draughts, darts), one country (the United States, the Netherlands) or one field of study (Mathematics, Physics, Economics, Statistics, Politics, Linguistics), and take a singular verb. A few of these (statistics, economics, politics) switch to a plural verb only when they mean actual data, calculations or political activities rather than the subject of study.

'One of the' and 'each of the' are always followed by a plural noun (one of the students, each of the students), never a singular one, because each picks a single member out of a group that must itself be named in the plural. The verb that follows 'one'/'each' later in the sentence still agrees with 'one'/'each' and stays singular.
rules.ok: One of the biggest problems facing the committee is funding.
rules.bad: One of the biggest problem facing the committee is funding.

rules.text: Two subjects joined by 'both ... and' always take a plural verb, with no exception for which subject sits nearer the verb (unlike either...or and neither...nor, which follow the nearer subject).
rules.ok: Both the manager and the clerk were present at the audit.
rules.bad: Both the manager and the clerk was present at the audit.

rules.text: A plural noun of money, distance, weight, time or height, coming after a number, takes a singular verb when the whole phrase is treated as one single amount rather than a count of separate items.
rules.ok: Ten kilometres is too far to walk every day.
rules.bad: Ten kilometres are too far to walk every day.

q-sva-each.cue: A blank before 'each / every / either / neither / everyone', often followed by 'of the ...' plus a plural noun.
q-sva-each.standard: Find the subject word (each, every, neither ...). Ignore the plural noun after 'of'. Choose the singular verb.
q-sva-each.fast: See 'each' or 'every' and go straight to the singular option: is, was, has.
q-sva-each.eliminate: Cross out every plural verb (are, were, have) before reading the rest.
traps: The plural noun after 'of' pulls the eye towards a plural verb.
'Every boy and every girl' still takes a singular verb.

q-sva-nearer.cue: 'Either ... or', 'neither ... nor', or two subjects joined by 'or' / 'nor'.
q-sva-nearer.standard: Look at the subject placed immediately before the verb. Match the verb to its number.
q-sva-nearer.fast: Read only the last subject and the blank.
q-sva-nearer.eliminate: Drop the options that agree with the first subject unless it is also the nearer one.
traps: Agreeing with the first subject because it is read first.
Reversing the order of subjects changes the correct verb.

q-sva-number.cue: 'The number of' or 'A number of' before a plural noun.
q-sva-number.standard: 'The number' is the subject: singular. 'A number of' works as 'many': plural.
q-sva-number.fast: 'The' keeps it singular, 'A' makes it plural.
q-sva-number.eliminate: Decide the article first (the or a). It fixes the number of the verb.
traps: Reading the plural noun that follows as the subject after 'the number of'.
Treating 'a number of' as a singular count.

q-sva-phrase.cue: A subject followed by 'along with', 'together with', 'as well as' or 'in addition to' and another noun, then the blank.
q-sva-phrase.standard: Cover the phrase between commas. The subject left is the one the verb agrees with.
q-sva-phrase.fast: Strike out the 'along with ...' phrase and read the sentence without it.
q-sva-phrase.eliminate: Remove every option that agrees with the noun inside the phrase.
traps: The nearer plural noun inside the phrase pulls the verb to the plural.
'And' would make a plural subject, but 'along with' does not.

q-sva-spot.cue: 'Find the part of the sentence that contains an error' over a long sentence where the verb is far from its subject or the subject begins with 'That', 'What' or 'Much'.
q-sva-spot.standard: Find the verb in each part. Locate its true subject by crossing out the commas, 'of ...' and 'on ...' phrases. Check number. The part with the mismatch is the error.
q-sva-spot.fast: Go to the part with the main verb (is/are/was/were or a verb with -s) and match it with the first noun of the sentence.
q-sva-spot.eliminate: Parts without a verb cannot be an agreement error; skip them.
traps: A plural noun just before the verb ('causes', 'overlaps') pulls the eye to a plural verb.
A clause subject starting with 'That' is singular.
'Much of' is singular.

q-sva-inverted.cue: A blank right after 'So + adjective' or 'Here/There', with the subject coming after the blank.
q-sva-inverted.standard: Turn the sentence round (The talks were so fragile ...), find the subject, and choose the verb that agrees with it and suits the tense.
q-sva-inverted.fast: Look right of the blank for the noun it agrees with.
q-sva-inverted.eliminate: Remove the verbs with the wrong number first; if two remain, decide by tense.
traps: Agreeing with the adjective before the blank.
When two options agree in number (are, were), the tense of the rest of the sentence decides.

q-sva-oneidea.cue: Two nouns or adjectives joined by 'and', describing what could be one thing or two (a dish, a quality, a person with several roles).
q-sva-oneidea.standard: Decide whether the pair names one thing or two separate ones. Check whether an article is repeated before each noun: repeated means two, not repeated means one.
q-sva-oneidea.fast: 'The X and Y' (one article) -> singular if X and Y are one entity; 'The X and the Y' -> plural.
q-sva-oneidea.eliminate: Drop the plural option once the pair is confirmed to be one idea, and vice versa.
traps: 'And' usually signals a plural subject, so the eye reaches for a plural verb even when the pair is one thing.
A famous saying ('slow and steady') is easy to mishear as two separate qualities.

q-sva-fixedplural.cue: A noun ending in -s that names a disease, a game, a country or a field of study.
q-sva-fixedplural.standard: Recognise the noun as one of the fixed list; ignore the final -s and use the singular verb, unless the sentence is clearly about data, sums, or political activity rather than the subject itself.
q-sva-fixedplural.eliminate: Drop every plural-verb option unless the noun is being used for actual data or activities, not the subject.
traps: The -s ending looks exactly like an ordinary plural noun.
'Statistics shows a rise' (the subject) vs 'The statistics are inflated' (the actual figures) take different verbs.

q-sva-ofthe.cue: 'One of the' directly followed by a noun, with the verb for that noun among the options.
q-sva-ofthe.standard: Make the noun right after 'the' plural; the verb that goes with 'one' itself, usually later in the sentence, still stays singular.
q-sva-ofthe.fast: One of the + always plural noun.
q-sva-ofthe.eliminate: Drop any option that keeps the noun right after 'one of the' singular.
traps: The singular-sounding 'one' misleads many into keeping the following noun singular too.
A long clause between 'one of the' and the main verb hides which noun the plural rule applies to.

q-sva-unit.cue: A number followed by a plural noun of money, distance, weight, time or height.
q-sva-unit.standard: Check whether the sentence treats the amount as one single quantity (a distance, a sum, a stretch of time) rather than as that many separate items; if so, use the singular verb.
q-sva-unit.fast: Ten kilometres/thousand rupees/five years + is/was, when read as 'that much altogether'.
q-sva-unit.eliminate: Drop the plural-verb option once the phrase is read as one amount rather than many separate units.
traps: The plural noun (kilometres, rupees, years) pulls the eye towards a plural verb even when the sentence means one total amount.

q-sva-both.cue: Two subjects joined by 'both ... and', with options differing in verb number (and sometimes tense).
q-sva-both.standard: A 'both ... and' subject is always plural, whichever of the two nouns sits nearer the verb; rule out every singular option first, then choose between the plural options by tense.
q-sva-both.fast: Both X and Y = always plural, no exceptions.
q-sva-both.eliminate: Drop every singular-verb option at once; the choice is only ever among the plural ones.
traps: Treating 'both ... and' like 'either ... or' and matching the nearer, sometimes singular, subject.
A singular option that otherwise sounds natural because the nearer noun is singular.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
That the report overlooked several underlying causes / behind the public unrest were surprising / given the volume of evidence / collected over the past few months.
options: That the report overlooked several underlying causes
behind the public unrest were surprising
collected over the past few months
pyqs.why: 'That the report overlooked several underlying causes behind the public unrest' is one noun clause acting as the subject, so the verb must be singular: 'was surprising'. 'Were' is wrong.

a.note: This is the start of the subject clause and is correct in itself.

c.note: 'Given the volume of evidence' is a phrase of reason and has no agreement problem.

d.note: 'Collected over the past few months' is a participle phrase about the evidence and is correct.

pyqs.trick: A 'That ...' clause is one singular subject.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Much of what seems to be coordination / among the regulatory bodies and private stakeholders / are, in reality, coincidental overlaps / arising from differing mandates.
options: Much of what seems to be coordination
among the regulatory bodies and private stakeholders
pyqs.why: The subject is 'much', which is singular, so the verb should be 'is'. 'Overlaps' is the complement and does not decide the number.

a.note: The subject 'much of what seems to be coordination' is correctly built.

b.note: 'Among the regulatory bodies and private stakeholders' is a prepositional phrase and has no verb to disagree.

d.note: 'Arising from differing mandates' is a participle phrase and is correct.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The report's focus on tech-utopianism, though praiseworthy, / ignore the deep-rooted inequities / that continue in data availability and digital competence / across demographic and regional gaps.
options: The report's focus on tech-utopianism, though praiseworthy,
that continue in data availability and digital competence
pyqs.why: The subject is the singular 'focus', so the verb must be 'ignores'. 'Tech-utopianism' and the 'though' phrase sit in between but do not change the number.

a.note: This part is the subject and the interrupting phrase and has no error.

c.note: 'That continue' looks wrong next to singular nouns, but its subject is the plural 'inequities', so 'continue' is correct.

d.note: 'Across demographic and regional gaps' is a prepositional phrase and is correct.

pyqs.trick: Strike the commas and 'on ...': focus ignores.

pyqs.text:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.
So fragile ___ the talks that one disclosure could sabotage them.
pyqs.why: The talks (plural) follow the blank, so the verb is plural. The sentence also uses 'could', a past form, so 'were' matches the tense.

a.note: 'Are' agrees with 'talks' but is present, while 'could sabotage' sets the sentence in the past.

c.note: Singular verb agreeing with 'fragile' instead of the plural subject 'talks' that follows.

d.note: Singular past verb: the tense is right, but the subject 'talks' is plural.

pyqs.caution: 'Are' agrees with 'talks' too, and a present-tense reading is grammatical. The printed key (were) rests on matching the past 'could'. Treat it as the answer expected in the exam, not as the only possible grammar.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
One of the most difficult problem / that the organisation faces / is the evasion of contribution / by small establishments.
options: One of the most difficult problem
pyqs.why: 'One of the' must be followed by a plural noun, so 'problem' should be 'problems'; the verb 'is' later in the sentence correctly stays singular, agreeing with 'one'.

b.note: 'That the organisation faces' is a correct relative clause.

c.note: 'Is the evasion of contribution' correctly keeps the singular verb for 'one'.

d.note: 'By small establishments' is a correct closing phrase.

pyqs.text:
Choose the best option to fill in the blank below.
Both Amia and Kavitha ___ hard for their Bank PO exams scheduled next month.
pyqs.why: 'Both Amia and Kavitha' always takes a plural verb, which rules out the singular 'has been studying' and 'is studying'; between the two plural options, the ongoing preparation for an exam still ahead is best read as a present perfect continuous action still in progress, so 'have been studying' fits better than the plain habitual 'study'.

a.note: 'Study' is plural and grammatically possible, but it reads as a general habit rather than the ongoing preparation the sentence describes.

c.note: 'Has been studying' is singular, pulled in by the nearer name 'Kavitha', but 'both ... and' always takes a plural verb regardless of which subject is nearer.

d.note: 'Is studying' is singular for the same reason, and also drops the sense of an action that has been continuing, not just happening right now.

pyqs.text:
Each sentence below stands on its own. Identify the one that contains a grammatical error.
Mitali's hair is long and black.
Either of the alternatives seem to present major difficulties.
One of the cars in the garage is fifty years old.
Sharon has six brothers.
options: Mitali's hair is long and black.
Either of the alternatives seem to present major difficulties.
One of the cars in the garage is fifty years old.
pyqs.why: 'Either' is the subject and is singular, so the verb must be 'seems'; the plural 'alternatives' after 'of' does not change it: 'Either of the alternatives seems to present major difficulties.'

a.note: 'Mitali's hair is long and black.' has the singular subject 'hair' correctly taking 'is'; there is no error here.

c.note: 'One of the cars in the garage is fifty years old.' has the singular subject 'One' correctly taking 'is'; 'of the cars' is only a prepositional phrase.

d.note: 'Sharon has six brothers.' is a correctly formed sentence with a singular subject and 'has'.

pyqs.trick: Either/neither/each/every + of + a plural noun still takes a singular verb.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Each of the student must bring their own lunch.
pyqs.why: 'Each of the' is always followed by a plural noun, so 'the student' must be 'the students'; the verb 'must bring' is unaffected since 'each' itself stays singular.

b.note: Choosing 'No error' misses the singular noun after 'each of the', which must be plural.

c.note: 'Must bring' is a correct modal plus bare verb; the fault lies earlier, in the noun's number.

d.note: 'Their own lunch' is a correct object phrase, using the common gender-neutral 'their' for 'each'.

pyqs.trick: Each of the + plural noun, just like one of the.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Each of the students ___ given a certificate.
practice.why: 'Each' is the subject and is singular; 'of the students' does not change that.

b.note: Plural verb chosen because 'students' sits next to the blank; the subject is 'each'.

c.note: Plural present form, pulled by 'students'; the subject 'each' needs a singular verb.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural; 'each' needs 'has been' or 'was'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Every boy and every girl in the class ___ invited to the party.
practice.why: Every before each noun keeps the subject singular even though 'and' joins two nouns.

a.note: Plural verb chosen because 'and' joins two nouns; 'every' before each noun keeps it singular.

c.note: Plural present verb, with the same pull from 'and'; the sentence is also in the past.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural; 'every' needs a singular verb.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Neither the teacher nor the students ___ aware of the change.
practice.why: The subject nearer to the verb is 'students' (plural), so the verb is plural.

a.note: Singular verb chosen to agree with 'teacher', the first subject, instead of the nearer 'students'.

b.note: Singular verb agreeing with 'teacher', the first subject, instead of the nearer 'students'.

d.note: Singular again, agreeing with 'teacher' rather than the nearer plural 'students'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Either the children or their mother ___ going to attend the function.
practice.why: The nearer subject is 'mother' (singular), so the verb is singular.

a.note: Plural verb chosen to agree with 'children', the first subject, not the nearer 'mother'.

c.note: Plural past verb agreeing with 'children'; the nearer subject 'mother' is singular.

d.note: Plural verb agreeing with 'children' rather than the nearer 'mother'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The number of unemployed youth ___ increasing every year.
practice.why: The subject is 'the number', which is singular.

a.note: Plural verb chosen because 'youth' is read as the subject; after 'the number of' the subject is 'number'.

c.note: Plural past verb: 'the number of' is singular, and 'every year' calls for the present.

d.note: Plural verb agreeing with 'youth'; the subject is the singular 'number'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
A number of passengers ___ waiting at the gate.
practice.why: 'A number of' means 'many', so the subject is plural.

a.note: Singular verb, as if the subject were 'the number'; 'a number of' means many and is plural.

b.note: Singular past verb, treating 'a number' as one count; it means many and is plural.

d.note: Singular verb: 'a number of passengers' is plural.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The principal, along with the teachers, ___ attending the seminar.
practice.why: The phrase 'along with the teachers' does not add to the subject; 'principal' is singular.

a.note: Plural verb pulled by 'teachers', the noun inside the 'along with' phrase.

c.note: Plural past verb pulled by 'teachers'; the real subject is 'principal'.

d.note: Plural verb pulled by 'teachers'; 'along with' does not make the subject plural.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The captain as well as the players ___ delighted with the win.
practice.why: 'As well as the players' is an extra phrase; the subject is the singular 'captain'.

b.note: Plural verb pulled by 'players' in the 'as well as' phrase.

c.note: Plural present verb pulled by 'players'; the sentence is also in the past.

d.note: Plural verb pulled by 'players'; the subject is the singular 'captain'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The list of candidates who cleared the interview / were pinned on the notice board / outside the office / on Monday morning.
options: The list of candidates who cleared the interview
were pinned on the notice board
practice.why: The subject is the singular 'list'; 'of candidates' is only a prepositional phrase, so the verb must be 'was pinned'.

a.note: 'The list of candidates who cleared the interview' is the subject with its relative clause, and 'cleared' agrees with the plural 'candidates'.

c.note: 'Outside the office' is a prepositional phrase with no verb in it.

d.note: 'On Monday morning' is a phrase of time and cannot hold an agreement error.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Neither of the two proposals / that the committee examined last week / seem workable / in the present budget.
options: that the committee examined last week
practice.why: 'Neither' is the subject and is singular, so the verb must be 'seems'; the plural 'proposals' after 'of' does not change it.

a.note: 'Neither of the two proposals' is correctly built as a singular subject.

b.note: 'The committee examined' looks like a mismatch next to a singular noun, but 'examined' is the same in both numbers, so there is no error here.

d.note: 'In the present budget' is a prepositional phrase with no verb.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
What the inspectors found in the two godowns / was reported to the head office, / but the quantities they recorded / was never checked again.
options: What the inspectors found in the two godowns
was reported to the head office,
practice.why: The subject of the last part is the plural 'quantities', so it needs 'were never checked'. The earlier singular 'was reported' is correct because its subject is the clause 'What the inspectors found'.

a.note: A 'What ...' clause is a correctly formed subject.

b.note: 'Was reported' looks wrong beside 'godowns', but its subject is the whole 'What ...' clause, which is singular.

c.note: 'But the quantities they recorded' is the subject of the last part and is correctly built.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Here ___ the documents you asked for.
practice.why: After 'here' the verb comes before its subject; the subject is the plural 'documents', so the verb is 'are'.

a.note: Singular verb chosen because it stands next to 'here'; the subject is the plural 'documents' that follows.

c.note: Singular and past; the subject is plural and the sentence is about the present moment.

d.note: 'Has been' is singular; the plural subject needs 'are'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
So heavy ___ the rain that the match was called off.
practice.why: The subject after the blank is the uncountable 'rain', which is singular, and the sentence is in the past.

a.note: Plural verb chosen by looking at 'heavy' rather than at the singular subject 'rain'.

c.note: Plural and present; the subject is singular and 'was called off' sets the sentence in the past.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural; the singular 'rain' needs 'was'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Slow and steady ___ the race, as the old fable reminds us.
practice.why: 'Slow and steady' names one combined quality (a way of behaving), not two separate subjects, so the verb is singular: wins.

a.note: Plural verb chosen because 'and' usually joins two subjects; here it joins two words describing one quality.

c.note: The continuous form is plural in number and does not fit this general truth, stated as a simple present.

d.note: 'Have won' is plural and also changes the sense from a general truth to a completed action.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Bread and butter / is / her only meal / every single morning.
practice.why: There is no error here. 'Bread and butter' names one dish, so the singular 'is' is correct, and the rest of the sentence is grammatical.

a.note: A correct subject naming one combined dish.

b.note: The singular verb correctly agrees with the one-dish subject.

c.note: A correct noun phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The Chairman and Managing Director ___ expected to address the shareholders today.
practice.why: With no article before 'Managing Director', the two titles belong to one person, so the verb is singular.

b.note: Plural verb chosen as though two different people were named; the missing second article shows this is one person holding both titles.

c.note: Plural and past; the sentence names one person and is about today.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural, which fits two people, not the one person this sentence names.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The teacher and the headmistress [[is attending]] the workshop together.
practice.why: The article is repeated before each noun ('the teacher' and 'the headmistress'), so they are two different people and the verb must be plural: are attending.

b.note: 'Is attend' is not a grammatical verb form.

c.note: 'Was attending' is singular and past; two people are named and the sentence is in the present.

d.note: 'Has attended' is singular, which fits one person, not the two different people named here.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Statistics ___ a compulsory subject for commerce students.
practice.why: Here 'Statistics' names the subject of study, not a set of figures, so it takes a singular verb.

b.note: Plural verb chosen because the word ends in -s; as the name of a subject, it is singular.

c.note: Plural and past; the subject is singular and the sentence is in the present.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural, which does not fit the subject-of-study sense of 'Statistics'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The figures he quoted / in the annual report / are inflated / by almost twenty percent.
practice.why: There is no error here. 'The figures' is an ordinary plural noun (not the subject 'Statistics'), so the plural 'are inflated' is correctly used, and the closing phrase is fine.

a.note: A correct subject using the ordinary plural noun 'figures'.

c.note: The plural verb correctly agrees with the plural 'figures'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Mumps ___ common among school-going children in winter.
practice.why: 'Mumps' names one disease and takes a singular verb, however plural it looks.

b.note: Plural verb chosen because 'Mumps' ends in -s; disease names like this stay singular.

c.note: Plural and past; the sentence describes a general, present fact.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural, which this singular disease name does not take.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
The West Indies [[are]] known for producing fast bowlers.
practice.why: 'The West Indies' is the name of one region/cricket team, so it takes a singular verb: is known.

b.note: 'Are know' is not a grammatical verb form.

c.note: 'Were known' is plural and past; the name is singular and this is a general present fact.

d.note: 'Have known' changes the sense to an action the West Indies performs, not a quality it is known for, and stays plural.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Fifty thousand rupees ___ a reasonable price for that old scooter.
practice.why: The sum is treated as one single amount, not fifty thousand separate rupees, so the verb is singular.

b.note: Plural verb chosen because 'rupees' is a plural noun; here the whole sum is one amount.

c.note: Plural and past; the sentence is a general statement about the present.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural, which does not fit a sum read as one amount.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Ten years / is a long time / to wait / for a single promotion.
practice.why: There is no error here. 'Ten years' is read as one stretch of time, so the singular 'is' is correctly used, and the rest of the sentence is grammatical.

a.note: A correct subject naming one span of time.

b.note: The singular verb correctly agrees with the one-span subject.

c.note: A correct non-finite phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Two kilograms of rice ___ enough to feed the whole family tonight.
practice.why: The two kilograms are treated as one quantity of rice, not two separate items, so the verb is singular.

b.note: Plural verb chosen because 'kilograms' is plural; here the whole weight is one quantity of rice.

c.note: Plural and past; the sentence is about tonight.

d.note: 'Have been' is plural, which does not fit a single quantity read as one amount.
